clue.text: Unbroken company detachment retreating in common sense

indicators.note: troops retreating move backwards, so the word they stand for is read backwards
'in' places one piece physically inside another, here inside NOUS

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
nous is British slang for practical good sense
a detachment is a military UNIT, turned round

explanation.surface: A company of soldiers retreats in an unbroken line, showing plain common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The military flavour of company, detachment and retreating makes the surface read as one scene, but only 'Unbroken' at the start is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something continuous runs on without a gap.

clue.text: Astronomical object with tail and wake incomplete

indicators.note: something incomplete lacks its finish, so the phrase loses its final letter

blocks.note: to wake is to COME TO; drop the final O

explanation.surface: An astronomer describes a heavenly body trailing a tail and a broken wake.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is part of the definition, not an instruction to take a last letter; the deletion signal is 'incomplete', acting on COME TO.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the tail of gas and dust is what marks out this body from other objects in the night sky.

clue.text: No reduction in jam, accommodating a large yearning

indicators.note: a reduction makes a word smaller, so STICK is cut short to STIC
to accommodate guests is to take them in, so STIC takes A LG inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
to jam is to STICK, reduced by its last letter
taken as written
LG is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A shopper insists on no discount on jam, with a big longing thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like preserve, but here it is the verb: when a drawer jams, it sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used as an adjective: a yearning look back at the past is a nostalgic one.

clue.text: Duplicates collapse of titanic swindle

indicators.note: a collapsed structure falls into pieces that can be rebuilt differently, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A huge fraud collapses because the fake documents are copies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' tempts you toward the ship, but here it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful sense: identical twins share the same genes, so each is in a way a duplicate of the other.

clue.text: Release American gin around November

indicators.note: 'around' puts one thing on both sides of another, so US is split to surround N

blocks.note: US is the abbreviation for American
N is November in the NATO alphabet
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: Someone releases an American gin in November, as if launching a new spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' is not the drink but a snare for animals, as in gin trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in a narrow sense: undoing a buckle or harness lets whatever was held go free.

clue.text: Free meal, no starter, central course (not starter)

indicators.note: the starter is the first course, so the word loses its first letter
again the first course, here the first letter, is left off

blocks.note: LUNCH without L
the MAIN course without M

explanation.surface: A menu offers a free meal: skip the starter and go straight to the main course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free meal' reads as one phrase, but Free is the definition, as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: taking off a prisoner's chains sets them at liberty.

clue.text: In favour of hosting University rowing crew, perhaps

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the house, so FOR takes U inside it

blocks.note: for = in favour of
U is the abbreviation for University

explanation.surface: Someone backs the University's hosting of a rowing crew.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Oxbridge rowing, which is also where the answer comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a four is a racing boat and its four oarsmen, one kind of rowing crew, as the 'perhaps' admits.

clue.text: Dislike sulphur being kept away from reactive metal

indicators.note: keeping the element away from the metal means taking its letter out of the word

blocks.note: sodium reacts violently with water
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur; it is removed

explanation.surface: A chemist keeps sulphur away from a reactive metal, out of dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is chemistry lab, but only 'Dislike' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, if a strong one: odium is widespread hatred.

clue.text: Medley of Lehar has listeners interrupting run-through

indicators.note: a medley mixes things, so the letters of LEHAR are mixed
an interruption breaks into the middle of something, so EARS breaks into the mixed letters

blocks.note: anagram of LEHAR
ears are what listen

explanation.surface: An orchestra's run-through of a Lehar medley is interrupted by the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Lehar was the composer of The Merry Widow, so 'medley' sounds like a musical term; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the theatre: a practice performance before the real show.

clue.text: Standard fashion regarding shirts in Northern town

blocks.note: stock = standard, as in a stock answer
ton = fashion, as in bon ton
on = about, regarding
tees are T-shirts

explanation.surface: A fashion report on the usual style of shirts worn in a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: TON for fashion is an old word from French, as in bon ton.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Stockton-on-Tees is a town in north-east England on the River Tees.

clue.text: People with servants reduced period in service

indicators.note: a reduced word is made shorter, so TERM loses its last letter
'in' places TER physically inside MASS

blocks.note: a mass is a church service
TERM cut short

explanation.surface: Staff complain that their period in service has been reduced by the people they work for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests domestic work, fitting the servants; here it is a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: in a household, the masters are the employers the servants answer to.

clue.text: Swimmer ready to keep fit with training

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so CASH holds the letters inside
training reshapes a body, so the letters of FIT are reshaped

blocks.note: ready money, or the readies, is cash
anagram of FIT

explanation.surface: A swimmer gets ready to keep fit through training.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimmer sounds like an athlete in training; it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a catfish is one creature that swims, a whiskered fish.

clue.text: Restaurant prosecution mostly about nothing after dessert returned

indicators.note: most but not all of the word is used, so TRIAL loses its last letter
'about' means surrounding, so TRIA goes around O
the prosecution piece comes after the dessert piece in the answer
something returned goes back, so TART is read backwards

blocks.note: a TART, turned round
a TRIAL, mostly
O = zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A restaurant faces prosecution after a dessert is sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' looks like a diner sending food back, which suits the restaurant; it is only the signal to reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a trattoria is a simple Italian restaurant.

clue.text: What’s the point of extra minute in sleep?

indicators.note: 'in' places M physically inside COMA

blocks.note: a coma is a deep sleep
M is the abbreviation for minute

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the point is of an extra minute in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grumble about lying in; the definition is a punctuation point.
explanation.definitionFit: A punning sense: 'point' is also a punctuation mark, and a comma is one.

clue.text: Feature of stage act? Compère’s introduced a good one

indicators.note: to introduce is to put in, so A, G and I are put into MC

blocks.note: a compère is an MC, master of ceremonies
A + G (good) + I (one)

explanation.surface: A compère introduces a good act on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A compère introducing acts is the host's job, so 'introduced' reads naturally; it is the container verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: a conjuror's stage act features magic.

clue.text: Unpleasant things in male mood — something burdensome

indicators.note: 'in' places the troubles physically inside the male

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
ills = troubles
tone = mood, as the tone of a meeting

explanation.surface: A man's gloomy mood is a heavy burden.
explanation.walkthrough: M is a single letter, so the container wraps the troubles and the mood piece simply follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a millstone round your neck is a heavy burden you cannot shed.

clue.text: Any pistol will shatter these locks

indicators.note: a shattered thing is smashed into pieces, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A gun that will blast open any lock.
explanation.walkthrough: The locks look like door locks a pistol might shoot open; they are locks of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A second sense of locks: tresses of hair, and ponytails are one way of wearing them.

clue.text: All but meaning to regulate press

indicators.note: 'all but' means everything except a little, so all of IMPORT except its last letter

blocks.note: IMPORT (meaning) without its T
to tune an engine is to regulate it

explanation.surface: A proposal to regulate the press, which means everything but that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspapers; it is the verb, to urge.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to press someone with repeated requests is to importune them.

clue.text: Nearby? Almost all close, I’d fancy

indicators.note: almost the whole word is used, so ALL loses its last letter
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are arranged freely

blocks.note: ALL, less one L
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone guesses a place is nearby, practically close, they fancy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' next to 'Nearby' looks like a synonym to swap in; it is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose sense, flagged by the question mark: what is localised is kept to a small area close at hand.

clue.text: Petitions involving two Conservatives beginning to see positive result

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so SUES takes the two Conservatives inside it
the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to sue is to petition a court
C is the abbreviation for Conservative, twice
first letter of see

explanation.surface: Two Tory petitions are starting to see a good outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petitions' is a verb here, as in petitions the court, not a list of signatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a success is an outcome that turned out well.

clue.text: Teeth study right to have change of heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so the middle letters of TRUE are changed round

blocks.note: a den is a private study
TRUE (right, correct) with its heart RU changed to UR

explanation.surface: A dental student studies teeth and has a change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' is literal: the heart of TRUE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the collective sense: a denture is a set of false teeth.

clue.text: Country network backed including recording

indicators.note: backed can mean moved back, so LAN is read backwards
to include is to hold within, so the reversed NAL holds EP

blocks.note: a LAN (local area network), reversed
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A rural broadcasting network supports a new recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' tempts you toward country music alongside network and recording; it is a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Nepal is one nation, in the Himalayas.

clue.text: Yellow stone, not dressed

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
raw, as undressed food or a salad without dressing

explanation.surface: A yellow stone left rough and unpolished.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is also a British unit of weight, 14 pounds, abbreviated ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A colour name: straw is the pale yellow of dried stalks.

clue.text: Weapon readily found round Lake

indicators.note: 'round' means encircling, so RIFE wraps around L

blocks.note: rife = widespread, readily found
L is the abbreviation for Lake

explanation.surface: A weapon is easily found near a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a bullet to go with the weapon; it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a rifle is one kind of firearm.

clue.text: Religious figure tucking into fish — curious problem

indicators.note: to tuck something into a space is to put it inside, so the religious figure goes inside the fish

blocks.note: the cod, a common fish
a nun is a religious figure
rum = odd, curious in old British slang

explanation.surface: A nun tucking into her fish supper makes a curious puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' suggests eating the fish; it means going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a conundrum is a puzzle, especially a hard one.

clue.text: Fine upset corporation importing chlorine

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down clue that turns the letters upside down
to import is to bring in, so TUM brings CL inside

blocks.note: corporation is jocular British slang for a paunch, a tum
Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine

explanation.surface: An upset corporation is fined for importing chlorine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' reads as a company, which fits the fine; it is an old joke for a pot belly. CL goes in after the T, then the lot is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to mulct someone is to fine them or take their money.

clue.text: What’s originating from criminal?

blocks.note: of = from, as in a man of Kent
a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what a criminal produces.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and read again it is also the wordplay: a word for 'originating from' followed by a kind of criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue asks what springs from a criminal, and the answer is the crime itself.

clue.text: Biased article in Paris — flinch when one’s put out

indicators.note: to put something out is to eject it, so the I is thrown out of QUAIL

blocks.note: une is a French indefinite article
QUAIL (flinch) with I (one) removed

explanation.surface: A biased report on a Paris article makes someone flinch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is I, the Roman numeral, dropped from QUAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: unequal treatment favours one side, which is what biased means.

clue.text: Energy certainly seen in storm centres

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
yes = certainly

explanation.surface: Energy is certainly visible at the heart of a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen' in the link sits neatly beside the answer, since eyes are what see.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical sense: the eye of a hurricane is the calm centre of the storm.

clue.text: Fools ecstatic tackling start of major tax process

indicators.note: a tackler wraps round the player, so SENT wraps round M
the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: asses = fools
sent = transported, ecstatic
first letter of major

explanation.surface: Delirious fools take on a big tax bill.
explanation.walkthrough: SENT for ecstatic is dated slang, as in music that sends you.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: a tax assessment is the process of working out what is owed.
